chunks: Whoever has a daughter is burdened; and whoever has two daughters — 'O, help from Allah!'; and whoever has three, jihad and every hardship is lifted from him; and whoever has four — O servants of God, help him! O servants of God, lend to him! O servants of God, have mercy on him!

And from him, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, from Abu Ayyub Sulayman ibn Muqbil al-Mada'ini, from Sulayman ibn Ja'far al-Ja'fari, from Abu al-Hasan al-Ridha (peace be upon him) who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said:

Indeed God, Blessed and Exalted, is more compassionate toward females than toward males; and there is no man who brings joy to a woman with whom he has a close relationship, except that God the Exalted will make him happy on the Day of Resurrection.

key_terms.أَرْأَفُ: More compassionate/gracious — God's greater mercy toward the female gender
key_terms.الْجِهَادُ: jihad — here meaning obligatory military struggle; the hadith says fathers of three daughters are exempted from this obligation
key_terms.حُرْمَةٌ: Sanctity/close relationship — refers to women related by kinship or marriage bonds, creating special obligations of care
key_terms.مَفْدُوحٌ: Burdened, overwhelmed — a term used to describe the challenging responsibility of providing for daughters in early Islamic society

ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet Muhammad say about the virtue of having daughters in Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated ultimately from the Prophet Muhammad (SAWW) through Imam al-Ridha (AS), extols the virtue of raising daughters and commands the community to support fathers of multiple daughters. The Prophet declares God's special compassion for females over males, and promises divine joy on the Day of Judgment to any man who brings happiness to a woman close to him. In pre-Islamic Arabian society, daughters were often seen as a burden, and this teaching directly challenged that attitude, reframing daughters as sources of spiritual merit and the father's station.
